historical_claims.anchor: On November 9, 1676, an astronomer at the Paris Observatory had a reason to watch Jupiter very carefully.
In 1610, Galileo Galilei turned a telescope toward Jupiter and noticed small points of light that changed position from night to night.
Earth rotates through fifteen degrees of longitude in one hour.
The innermost of Galileo's four large moons, Io, completes an orbit in about one day and eighteen hours:
He traveled to the island of Hven, between modern Denmark and Sweden, to compare observations from the site of Tycho Brahe's former observatory with observations made in Paris.
Giovanni Domenico Cassini, one of the observatory's leading figures, made eclipse tables and had already encountered discrepancies between the predicted and observed times.
The extent of his contribution to the decisive claim has been debated by historians examining the academy's records.
and the observation on November 9 corresponded to it.
On November 21 he presented the argument to the academy.
Rømer estimated that light would take roughly twenty-two minutes to cross a distance equal to the diameter of Earth's orbit.
A few decades later, astronomers found another way that finite light speed makes itself visible.
In 1849, Hippolyte Fizeau measured light travel time along a terrestrial route with a rapidly rotating toothed wheel and a distant reflector.
In 1983, the international body responsible for the metric system redefined the meter in terms of the distance light travels in vacuum during a specified fraction of a second.
A GPS satellite broadcasts a radio signal that includes information about when the signal was sent and where the satellite was.
From an orbit more than twenty thousand kilometers above Earth, a signal typically takes over sixty milliseconds to reach the ground.
The GPS receiver is also a lesson in everything that has become more complicated since Rømer's day.
Rømer returned to Copenhagen in 1681, helped improve astronomical instruments, worked on standards of weights and measures and took on substantial public duties.
Much of his unpublished observational material was lost in Copenhagen's great fire of 1728, after his death.
In reality, Io is a violent and fascinating world: a body reshaped by tidal heating, with volcanoes erupting across its surface.

claim_evidence.anchor: The delay would occur between the moon and the observer.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: The light-time correction changes with the Earth-Jupiter distance, whereas the physical eclipse time does not depend on the Earth observer.

claim_evidence.anchor: A small increase in the travel time from eclipse to eclipse accumulated into minutes over a season.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Each observed Io event includes the varying propagation time, yielding accumulated apparent drift.

claim_evidence.anchor: There are complications. Earth and Jupiter both move, so the distance between them changes in a more elaborate way than a simple picture of Earth sitting at the two opposite ends of a straight line.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: The 2 AU baseline is a convenient approximation; real geometric and orbital effects must be modeled.

claim_evidence.anchor: The modern value for that distance is about sixteen minutes and forty seconds.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Modern diameter-orbit light-travel time is around 998 seconds, often rounded to 16m40s.

claim_evidence.anchor: To turn a travel duration into a speed measured in kilometers per second, one also needs the length of the route in kilometers.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: The inferred physical speed depends on the solar-system distance scale.

claim_evidence.anchor: The apparent direction shifted over the year, but the timing was wrong for the explanation they had been looking for.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Bradley discovered annual stellar aberration rather than the sought parallax.

claim_evidence.anchor: A modern satellite navigation receiver encounters a related problem whenever it calculates your location.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: GPS solves satellite-range and receiver-clock offset from radio propagation times.

description: A late eclipse of Jupiter’s moon Io led Ole Rømer to argue in 1676 that light needed time to cross space. From astronomical longitude tables and Cassini’s objections to stellar aberration, Fizeau’s wheel, the modern metre and GPS, this essay follows what a changing signal delay can reveal.
